newsitem.title: NORWAY: Norway premier is home-grown Labour Party product.
newsitem.headline: Norway premier is home-grown Labour Party product.

text.p: Thorbjoern Jagland, who succeeded Gro Harlem Brundtland as Norway's prime minister on Friday, is a pure-bred product of the ruling Labour Party, the country's most powerful political group.

Jagland, 46, is also a typical Norwegian politician who does not lose sight of family life: he went shopping for a birthday present in the middle of hectic talks on the make-up of his new government the day before he took office.

Groomed as Brundtland's heir-apparent for four years, Jagland has spent his career moving through the ranks of the party, a centre-left movement that combines a passionate concern with social welfare and a strong interest in keeping private industry flourishing.

Recent opinion polls have shown that voters would turn their backs on the Labour Party with Jagland at the helm. But such surveys say more about Brundtland's standing with the Norwegian public than about distrust of Jagland.

"It is not easy to succeed a prime minister who has become the country's property. It may take time before Norway becomes on first-name terms with Thorbjoern as it has become with Gro," the national news agency NTB said.

Brundtland, 57, who has dominated politics for 15 years, had said she was thinking of stepping down. Yet it came as a surprise when she announced on Wednesday that she was resigning in two days to give Jagland and the Labour Party he chairs time to prepare properly for the next election in September 1997.

Financial markets were initially wary of Jagland, a politician with a left-wing background and whose support for continued state ownership of some industry and the country's top commercial banks has won him few friends in the markets.

But investors appeared to calm down after Jagland, whose political idol is late West German Chancellor Willy Brandt, said economic and other policies would remain unchanged in oil-rich Norway, one of the wealthiest states in Europe and still aloof from the 15-member European Union.
Jagland's down-to-earth manner is another sign of continuity in a country where politicians behave like ordinary people.

Taking a break from the government talks on Thursday, Jagland went shopping in downtown Oslo. "I need to go out and buy new hiking boots," the next prime minister told reporters. "I am going to receive them as a present from my wife on my birthday on November 5."
Jagland was born in Drammen, just west of the Norwegian capital Oslo, on November 5, 1950. His first senior position came in 1977 as leader of the AUF, Labour's youth league.

In 1981, the year Brundtland first became prime minister, Jagland was busy building a powerbase in the party. In 1992, he was voted in as party leader following Brundtland's resignation from the post after her son committed suicide.
Brundtland had initially wanted Jens Stoltenberg, industry and energy minister in her outgoing cabinet, as party leader and heir-apparent.
But Jagland won out because he was supported by the trade unions, traditional and powerful allies of the Labour Party.
The following year Jagland took over as parliamentary representative for the county of Buskerud.
Jagland is married with two sons, Anders and Henrik, and his family clearly comes first.

He turned down a golden chance to work in Brundtland's office in 1986 as a junior minister, saying he needed time with his children -- another typical feature of Norway where eight out of 10 men use their right to take paid paternity leave.
